name: Chloe Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the office for a family plumbing and heating firm, six engineers and a portacabin on a trading estate outside town. I take the calls, book the boiler services, plan who goes where each day, chase invoices and keep the gas safety certificates filed. Gary (the owner) is sixty-three and still does call-outs himself, and his son Lee runs the vans.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady and I know everyone, and I can tell from a customer's voice whether it's a real emergency or just a dripping tap. What wears me out is winter, when every boiler in the county breaks the same week and I'm on the phone from seven till six. The pay's lower than a big firm would pay, and I share a rented house with my sister, so after bills I've got maybe three weeks of money if something went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped, and now we can stop talking about it. I'd say that at the tea break and leave it there. I'm not really one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief. My job is phones and paper and knowing people, and I like it the way it is. The only thing nagging me is Gary retiring, because Lee keeps talking about booking apps, and that would happen with or without some big AI change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, the paper diary plus the spreadsheet. If Lee brings in a booking app, I'd ask him to show me once, slowly, and I'd still keep the paper diary as a backup. I'd also try to stop spending on lunches out, because there's never any money left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. More the feeling of things slowly shifting under me while I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your job if Gary sells up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Lee takes over, I think I'm fine, because he needs someone to run the office. If the firm gets sold to one of the big heating companies, they've got a call centre two hundred miles away. Then I'm looking for work in a town with maybe three office jobs going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you talked to Gary about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it feels rude to ask a man when he's retiring. I might ask Lee, casually, over a brew. I'd rather know than guess.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped** and we can stop talking about it.
I'd keep it to the **tea break**, not online.
think: My job is **phones, paper** and knowing people, and I like it that way.
The real worry is the owner **retiring** and the firm being sold.
do: Keep the **paper diary** and spreadsheet as they are.
Ask Lee to show me any **booking app** once, slowly.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if things are slowly shifting while I'm busy.
S0.quote: If the firm gets sold to one of the big heating companies, they've got a call centre two hundred miles away.
fieldNote: Chloe's worry is **succession** at the firm, not AI itself.
She'd accept a new app only if shown **slowly**, and keep paper as backup.
A sale would leave her job hunting in a town with about **three office jobs**.

steps.text: Keep the paper diary and spreadsheet for booking engineers
Stop buying lunch out on workdays
Wait to hear from Lee whether Gary plans to sell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should go carefully and not throw out people who know the customers. Some of it might be useful, I'm not against everything. But I'd say it plainly at work: a boiler customer at seven in the morning wants a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's my job, in the list on that card. Booking, answering customers, chasing invoices. If Lee got an app that books engineers and answers the phone, he'd keep me for a while out of loyalty, then maybe part-time, and I can't live on part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Lee straight out what he's planning, in the first month. I'd make myself do one of those free computer courses at the library, even though I'd hate it. And I'd look at the job adverts every week, though I know there's not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight, because I'm the one in the office who doesn't use any of this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you picked up the AI tools before now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust them, and I never needed them. I tried one once to write a complaint letter and it sounded like a robot apologising. I'd rather write it myself in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the job went part-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for evening shifts at the supermarket to top it up. My sister would help with rent for a month or two, but she's not rich either. It would be grim, honestly.

say: I'd say firms should keep people who **know the customers**.
I'd say a boiler customer at seven wants **a human**.
think: Booking, **answering customers** and invoices are my job, listed on the card.
The firm might cut me to **part-time**, which I can't live on.
do: Ask Lee **straight out** what he plans in the first month.
Take a free **computer course** at the library.
feel: **Alarmed**, because I'm the only one in the office not using AI.
S1.quote: I'm the one in the office who doesn't use any of this stuff.
fieldNote: Chloe recognises her **own tasks** on the card and drops her calm tone.
She'd force herself through a **library course** despite strong distrust.
Part-time hours would mean **supermarket shifts** and leaning on her sister.

steps.text: Take the free computer skills course at the library
Check local job adverts every week for office work
Ask her sister to cover more rent if hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody needs to slow this down, because two years is ridiculous. I'm not a protest person, but I'd sign the petitions. I'd tell people at work it's not their fault if they can't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished in office work by 2028. I don't know what I'd do. The engineers keep going until the robots come about three years later, but nobody needs someone like me ringing them with their jobs any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. Maybe ask Gary if I could train as a plumber's mate, because that's three more years of work at least. Cut everything to the bone. Move back in with my mum if the rent goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, honestly. I can feel it in my stomach just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said plumber's mate. Would you really do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. I've watched the lads enough to know how a boiler service goes. It would be awful at first, but it's work, and I'd rather be in a loft than on the dole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm scared and I don't have a plan. She works at a bank branch, so she's probably worse off than me. We'd sit in the kitchen and have no idea what to say.

say: I'd say someone needs to **slow this down**, because two years is ridiculous.
I'd sign **petitions**, though I'm not a protest person.
I'd tell colleagues it's **not their fault** if they can't keep up.
think: The engineers last until the **robots**, about three years later.
I honestly **don't know** what I'd do next.
do: Ask Gary about training as a **plumber's mate**.
Move back to **my mum's** if rent can't be paid.
S2.quote: I'd rather be in a loft than on the dole.
fieldNote: Chloe has **no plan** and no savings, so the short warning overwhelms her.
She sees the engineers' **three-year gap** and reaches for it as a plumber's mate.
Her sister works at a **bank branch**, so the household faces two hits.

steps.text: Ask Gary to take her on as a plumber's mate
Cut spending to rent, food and the bus
Move back in with her mum if rent can't be met
Sign petitions to slow the AI rollout down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be sensible about it. Firms should train their people, not just bin them. I'd say that to Gary and Lee, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit more room, but I know I'd be slow. My office work still goes by 2031. If I started now, a trade gives me a few years working before the robots, but a trade is not a career, it's a delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gary about the plumbing apprenticeship, maybe a part-time one, while still doing the office. I'd try to save something every month, even fifty. And I'd stop pretending this isn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Less of a punch than two years, but it's the same ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop pretending. What does pretending look like for you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keeping the paper diary because it's comfortable. Saying I'm too busy for courses. I know I do it, and I'd have to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Gary pay for the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might, he's fair. He's said before he wishes more young people went into the trade. If he did, I'd owe him a lot.

say: I'd say firms should **train their people**, not bin them.
I'd say it **politely** to Gary and Lee.
think: A trade now is more a **delay** than a career.
Five years gives a bit **more room**, but I know I'd be slow.
do: Ask Gary about a **part-time plumbing apprenticeship**.
Stop putting off **courses** as too busy.
feel: **Alarmed** still, a smaller punch but the same ending.
S3.quote: A trade gives me a few years working before the robots, but a trade is not a career, it's a delay.
fieldNote: Chloe names her own **avoidance**: the comfortable paper diary and 'too busy' for courses.
She sees the trade as a **delay**, so the extra years don't lift her mood.
She trusts Gary to be **fair**, which shapes her plan.

steps.text: Start a part-time plumbing apprenticeship alongside the office work
Save fifty pounds a month towards a cushion
Ask Gary for help with the apprenticeship fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to sort it out properly, if people get on with it. I'd tell the younger ones to pick something with their hands. I'd be calmer about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm thirty-seven. That's young enough to learn a full trade properly and have a few good years in it. I'm still nervous, because I'm slow with new things, but ten years is enough even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the plumbing apprenticeship within a couple of years, once I'd saved a bit. I'd keep the office job until then. I'd also start using the booking app Lee wants, so I'm not left behind while I'm still in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some room to breathe. It's a long time to get used to an idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a couple of years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I need some money behind me first. Apprentice pay is lower, and I can't drop to that with three weeks in the bank. If I save for two years, I could do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think it would actually go to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not exactly. Something always breaks, like the car or the boiler at home, ironically. But I'd at least have a plan written down, which is more than I've got now.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if people **get on with it**.
I'd tell younger people to pick **hands-on work**.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could learn a full trade properly.
I'm **slow with new things**, but ten years is enough.
do: Save for **two years**, then start the plumbing apprenticeship.
S4.quote: Apprentice pay is lower, and I can't drop to that with three weeks in the bank.
fieldNote: The long warning lets Chloe **save first**, which is the real change.
She agrees to use the **booking app**, a big step for her.
She still expects the **office job** to go, so stays anxious.

steps.text: Save for two years before starting a plumbing apprenticeship
Use Lee's new booking app for engineer schedules
Keep running the firm's office until the switch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no plan and no money, and I'm slow with new things. What would help is being paid something while I learned a trade, even a basic wage, and firms being given a reason to train their staff instead of letting them go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small firms. Everyone pictures big offices, but a lot of us work in portacabins for one family. When the owner retires, the whole job depends on one conversation over a cup of tea.

headlineQuote: When the owner retires, the whole job depends on one conversation over a cup of tea.
portrait: Chloe is **27**, running the office of a family plumbing firm on a trading estate, sharing a rented house with her sister.
She has about **three weeks** of money and few office jobs nearby.
She **never uses AI** and prefers a paper diary, but admits this is avoidance.
She's practical and **centre-minded**: wants firms to train staff and things done sensibly.
She panics at two years and sees a **plumbing trade** as a delay that buys time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no plan, no money and being slow with change.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic wage** while learning a trade.
Reasons for firms to **train staff** instead of letting them go.
